interactions.label: Dr. Rao is the most senior consultant in the ward but never personally treated o

params.question: Dr. Rao is the most senior consultant in the ward but never personally treated or examined a patient who has just died. Dr. Mehta, a junior colleague, was the primary treating doctor throughout the admission. Who should sign the MCCD?

answers.text: Dr. Rao, because seniority carries the authority to certify any death in the department

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Seniority alone does not qualify a doctor to certify a death. The MCCD requires personal knowledge of the case — attendance during the final illness or personal examination of the body.

answers.text: Dr. Mehta, because personal knowledge of the case through direct treatment is mandatory to certify

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969 requires the certifying doctor to have personally attended the deceased during the final illness or examined the body afterward — Dr. Mehta meets this, Dr. Rao does not.

answers.text: Either doctor may sign, since both work in the same clinical department

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Working in the same department does not confer eligibility. Only a doctor with direct, personal involvement in that specific patient's care may certify.

answers.text: The hospital's medical superintendent, since administrative sign-off is required for all deaths

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The medical superintendent has no special certifying role here. The MCCD must be signed by the attending registered medical practitioner with personal knowledge of the case.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: the RBD Act 1969 requires personal knowledge of the case (treatment during final illness or post-mortem examination) before a doctor may sign the MCCD.
Right — personal involvement in the patient's care, not rank, determines who may certify.

interactions.label: While completing an MCCD and assigning the ICD-11 code, from which part of the c

params.question: While completing an MCCD and assigning the ICD-11 code, from which part of the certificate should you identify the condition to code as the underlying cause of death?

answers.text: The topmost row of Part I, since it lists the immediate cause

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The topmost row (Ia) is the immediate cause — the final mechanism, not the underlying disease process. Coding this alone would make many different diseases look statistically identical.

answers.text: The lowest occupied row of Part I

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The underlying cause — the condition that started the chain leading to death — is found in the lowest completed row of Part I, and it is this condition that ICD-11 codes.

answers.text: Any condition listed in Part II

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Part II records significant conditions that contributed to death but were not part of the direct causal chain — these are not what gets ICD-11 coded as the underlying cause.

answers.text: Whichever condition appears most clinically severe, regardless of its position on the form

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Severity is not the criterion. ICD-11 coding follows the certificate's structured causal chain, always taking the lowest occupied row of Part I as the underlying cause.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the three-step process: find the lowest occupied row of Part I, search that condition in the ICD-11 browser, then pick the most specific code.
Correct — the lowest completed row of Part I is what drives ICD-11 coding and mortality statistics.

interactions.label: A 55-year-old man is brought to hospital after a road traffic accident and dies

params.question: A 55-year-old man is brought to hospital after a road traffic accident and dies within an hour of admission, before his internal injuries are fully confirmed. Can the treating doctor issue the MCCD directly?

answers.text: Yes, because the doctor personally examined him after the accident

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Personal examination alone is not enough — this is an unnatural death (accidental), which must be referred for police/magistrate involvement and forensic autopsy regardless of examination.

answers.text: No — this is an unnatural death requiring referral for police/magistrate process and forensic autopsy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Any accidental, homicidal, or suicidal death is unnatural and must go through the medicolegal route — the treating doctor cannot certify it directly.

answers.text: Yes, because death occurred inside the hospital under medical observation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Location of death does not override the unnatural-death rule. A road traffic accident death remains medicolegal even if it occurs on hospital premises.

answers.text: No, but only because he was admitted less than 24 hours ago — the accident itself is not disqualifying

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This reasoning is incomplete. The road traffic accident makes it an unnatural death in its own right, independent of the 24-hour admission rule.

overallFeedback.feedback: Any unnatural death (accidental, homicidal, or suicidal) mandates referral for forensic autopsy before any certificate is completed.
Right — unnatural deaths, including road traffic accidents, must always be referred, never certified directly.

interactions.label: Brain death was already a legally recognised basis for organ donation in India w

params.question: Brain death was already a legally recognised basis for organ donation in India well before the Transplantation of Human Organs Act (THOTA) was passed in 1994.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Actually false. Although brain death was clinically recognised since the 1960s, it lacked any legal status until THOTA 1994 formally legalised it for organ donation purposes.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — false. Brain death had been used clinically since the 1960s, but it had no legal standing in India until THOTA 1994 gave it legal recognition, enabling deceased-donor transplantation.

interactions.label: A man wishes to donate his kidney to his sister-in-law (his spouse's sibling), w

params.question: A man wishes to donate his kidney to his sister-in-law (his spouse's sibling), who does not fall on the 2011-amended near-relative list. What must happen before this donation can proceed?

answers.text: Only the donor's signed consent is needed, since donation is voluntary

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Consent alone is sufficient for near-relative donors, but a sister-in-law does not qualify as a near relative, so additional scrutiny is legally required.

answers.text: The hospital's transplant team can approve it directly, exactly as for a near-relative donor

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Direct transplant-team approval applies only to near-relative donors. A non-relative donor case must go to the Authorisation Committee instead.

answers.text: The case must be reviewed and approved by the Authorisation Committee to confirm the donation is genuinely voluntary and not commercial

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Non-relative donors with only an emotional connection require Authorisation Committee review specifically to rule out a disguised commercial transaction.

answers.text: Approval is automatic once the donor's medical fitness is confirmed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Medical fitness is necessary but not sufficient. Non-relative donations additionally require Authorisation Committee scrutiny of consent and motive.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall: only the defined near-relative list gets simplified transplant-team consent; everyone else, including emotionally connected non-relatives, goes to the Authorisation Committee.
Correct — non-relative donors need Authorisation Committee approval precisely because the relationship doesn't automatically establish a non-commercial motive.

interactions.label: A poor labourer sells his kidney to pay off a debt and signs the hospital's cons

params.question: A poor labourer sells his kidney to pay off a debt and signs the hospital's consent form before surgery. Analysing this through the principle of autonomy, why does this situation still raise an ethical concern despite the signed consent?

answers.text: The consent form is legally invalid because only near-relatives are permitted to donate kidneys

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This misstates the law — non-relative and even commercial-context donors can sign valid consent forms; the issue here is not who is allowed to donate but whether the consent is truly free.

answers.text: Genuine autonomy requires freedom from coercion, and severe financial pressure undermines that freedom even when a form is signed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. True autonomous consent requires both understanding and freedom from coercion. Economic desperation can make a 'voluntary' signature effectively coerced — which is exactly why THOTA bans payment and requires Authorisation Committee review.

answers.text: Non-maleficence is violated because kidney donation always causes serious, irreversible harm to any donor

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This overstates the surgical risk and misapplies the principle being tested here — the ethical problem in this scenario is compromised autonomy from financial coercion, not an absolute claim about donor harm.

answers.text: Beneficence is violated because the recipient did not pay the donor a fair market price

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Payment for organs is illegal under THOTA regardless of the 'price' — beneficence concerns the benefit to the recipient, not a fair-trade argument for organ sale.

overallFeedback.feedback: Focus on autonomy: informed consent must also be free of coercion. Severe financial pressure can invalidate the 'voluntary' nature of a signed consent form.
Right — real autonomy needs freedom from coercion, and financial desperation compromises that even with a signature, which is why commercial organ transactions are criminalised.
